title: I built a dating strategy sim with Claude where a smile doesn't mean yes. The idea came from an AI-to-AI dating experiment.
author: cutextwinklexcool
selftext:
I'm a solo developer, and Love Addict just came out on itch.io. I designed the game and directed every part of it. The code and the writing were done with Claude, the character art with Canva AI, and the music with Google Gemini (Lyria). The English text, and this post, were translated with AI.



The idea came from an experiment where two AIs went on a mock date and were then asked, separately, how it went. During the conversation Claude was full of praise for its partner. Afterward it rated the chance of a relationship at 1 out of 10. That gap between how someone acts and what they actually think became the core of the game. Every character quietly cares about a few things, smiles through your mistakes, and keeps score anyway. Your job is to read them before you make a move.



The hardest part of working with Claude was the opposite problem. An AI writer tends to make every character warm and agreeable, which kills a game about hidden opinions. I ended up writing rules for each character's reactions so that a polite reply and a real yes look different only in small details, and then checking the lines by hand.



The other thing that helped was having Claude write scripts that play the game automatically for decades of in-game time. Those runs caught balance problems in the money system, and a browser crash that only showed up after very long sessions.



It's a single HTML file that runs in the browser, with a small Cloudflare server for cross-device saves and monthly rankings. Everyone is drawn as an animal, and species tells you nothing about personality.



Free demo: [https://cutextwinklexcool.itch.io/love-addict-trial](https://cutextwinklexcool.itch.io/love-addict-trial)

Full game (50% off until Dec 2): [https://cutextwinklexcool.itch.io/love-addict](https://cutextwinklexcool.itch.io/love-addict)



Happy to answer questions about the workflow.

comments.author: TailorGame
comments.body: The point about an AI writer making every character warm and agreeable is a useful one, and writing per-character reaction rules so a polite reply and a real yes only differ in small details sounds like the right fix. Having Claude run automated playthroughs across decades of in-game time to find economy balance issues and the long-session crash is a smart use of it too. Did you find the hidden-opinion cues readable enough for players without them being obvious?

replies.author: cutextwinklexcool
replies.body:
Thanks, that's the part I'm least sure about, honestly.



Every reply comes with a short "(How they seem)" line: their smile is a little stiff, they sit closer than last time, they start to pull their hand back. Most of the read comes from those small details, not from what they actually say. A polite "Haha, sounds fun" and a real yes can look almost the same until you notice which one came with the stiff smile.



To keep it fair, the game shows you everything at the end: what each person actually cared about, how close your guesses were, and the moment that moved them most. So you can check whether the cues were there or you just missed them.



Whether that balance is right for new players, I don't know yet. If you'd be willing to give it a try, I'd really love to hear which cues felt too obvious and which ones you missed completely.
